passage:
At the dinner table, Papa was on the phone with Nilesh Uncle, saying something about the electricity bill. Jahnavi, five, waved her spoon. "Papa! Papa! Today at school Pihu's rabbit..."
Papa held up a finger to Nilesh Uncle, then put a warm hand on Jahnavi's arm and mouthed, "One minute." Jahnavi's mouth stayed open. She nodded hard. Her feet swung under the table, but she stayed quiet, pressing her lips together.
When the call ended, Papa turned. "Now. Tell me everything about the rabbit."
Jahnavi took a deep breath. "It ate a whole carrot in one bite!"

qa.q: What did Papa do when Jahnavi called out during the phone call?
qa.a: Papa held up a finger to Nilesh Uncle, then put a warm hand on Jahnavi's arm and mouthed "One minute."

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling while pressing her lips together and swinging her feet?
qa.a: Jahnavi was bursting with excitement and worried the news might vanish. The swinging feet and the deep nod show how hard it was to wait.

qa.q: What small signal did Papa use, and why did it work?
qa.a: Papa put a warm hand on the arm and mouthed "One minute", then came back to Jahnavi at once. The signal taught waiting without silencing her.

qa.q: How might Nilesh Uncle have felt during the interruption?
qa.a: Nilesh Uncle probably waited politely, and Papa's raised finger showed him it would be brief. He would not have minded a small pause.

grounding: A child interrupts because a thought feels urgent, and a hand on the arm teaches waiting without silencing them.

"Abbu, Abbu, look, look, a red truck!" Tarun tugged Imran's sleeve at the bus stop, though Imran was still talking to the neighbour.
"One second, beta." Imran rested a hand on Tarun's shoulder. "That's our signal. Hand on shoulder means I heard you and I'm coming."
"But it will go!"
"It will still be there. Count to five in your head."
Tarun counted, wriggling. "One, two, three, four, five."
Imran turned and crouched. "Now. Tell me about the truck."
"It was red and it had a ladder!"
"A ladder! Good spotting."

qa.q: What colour was the truck Tarun saw?
qa.a: The truck was red.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when saying "But it will go!"?
qa.a: Tarun was excited and afraid the thought would vanish, so waiting felt impossible. Wriggling while counting shows how strong the urge was.

qa.q: What did Imran do that helped Tarun learn to wait?
qa.a: Imran used a hand on the shoulder as a signal, asked Tarun to count to five and then gave full attention. Tarun was heard, not silenced.

qa.q: How might Imran's neighbour have felt during the interruption?
qa.a: The neighbour probably waited patiently for a moment, since Imran only asked for one second. The short pause was easy to understand.

grounding: A child interrupts because a thought feels urgent, and a hand signal teaches waiting without silencing them.

passage:
At the kindergarten, it was circle time, and Sarita Miss was telling the story of the thirsty crow.
Chinmay's hand shot up, then his whole body. "Miss! Miss! My grandpa has a crow! It comes to our window! It—"
Sarita Miss didn't say "Wait" or "Shh." She put a gentle hand on his arm, smiled, and kept reading one more line.
Chinmay jiggled, but waited, hand under hers.
When the crow dropped the last pebble, she turned to him. "Now, Chinmay. Tell us about your grandpa's crow."
He told everyone. It eats roti.

qa.q: What does the crow at Chinmay's window eat?
qa.a: It eats roti.

qa.q: Why did Chinmay's hand shoot up in the middle of the story?
qa.a: Chinmay was excited and eager, afraid his thought about Grandpa's crow might vanish if he waited.

qa.q: What did Sarita Miss's hand on his arm do?
qa.a: It told him she had seen him and his turn would come, so he could wait without being silenced.

qa.q: How might the other children see Sarita Miss's way of handling it?
qa.a: They likely felt the story wasn't spoiled and that everyone's thoughts are welcome, just at the right moment.

grounding: A child interrupts because a thought feels urgent, and a hand on the arm teaches waiting without silencing him.

passage:
Monday. Yamini was talking to the vegetable vendor when Yash tugged her dupatta. "Mumma! Mumma! The dog has spots!" She lost her place and snapped, "Wait, Yash!" He sulked all the way home.
Wednesday. At home Yamini said, "When I'm talking and you have something big to say, put your hand on my arm. I'll put my hand on yours. That means, I see you, you're next."
Friday. On the phone with Nani, Yamini felt a small hand on her arm. She covered it with her own. Yash bounced but waited.
"Okay, Yash, tell me."
"The dog had seven spots. I counted."

qa.q: How many spots did the dog have?
qa.a: The dog had seven spots.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling on Monday after Yamini snapped?
qa.a: Yash felt hurt and grumpy, sulking all the way home after his exciting news was brushed off.

qa.q: Why did the hand signal work?
qa.a: It let Yash show his urgent thought without interrupting, and Yamini's hand on his told him his turn was coming.

qa.q: What was Friday like for Yamini compared to Monday?
qa.a: On Friday Yamini could finish her call calmly and still feel close to Yash, without snapping.

grounding: A child interrupts because a thought feels urgent, and a hand signal teaches waiting without silencing him.

passage:
Rain hammered the tin roof of the small flat, and Papa, Ojas, was on an important work call, pacing by the window.
Nitin ran in. "Papa! Papa! The water is coming in under the door!"
Ojas held up a finger and said into the phone, "One second, sir." He crouched, put a hand on Nitin's arm and looked right at him.
"Show me."
Nitin pulled him to the door. There was a puddle.
Ojas stuffed a towel along the crack and said, "Good you told me. Next time, put your hand on my arm, and I'll come as soon as I can."
Nitin nodded, proud.

qa.q: What was coming in under the door?
qa.a: The water was coming in under the door.

qa.q: How did Nitin feel after Papa praised him?
qa.a: Nitin felt proud that telling Papa about the water had been the right thing to do.

qa.q: What did Ojas teach Nitin for next time?
qa.a: To put a hand on Papa's arm, a small signal that means Papa has seen him and will come as soon as possible.

qa.q: What might Ojas have been feeling when Nitin ran in during the call?
qa.a: Ojas might have felt torn and a little stressed, pulled between the important call and his son's urgent news.

grounding: A child interrupts because his news feels urgent, and a hand-on-arm signal teaches waiting without silencing him.

passage: At the Chennai bus stop, Harsha was asking the conductor about the route when Vishal tugged her sleeve. "Amma! Amma! Amma, the bus has a elephant painted—" "One minute, kanna." "But AMMA—" Harsha didn't scold. She put Vishal's small hand on her arm and covered it with hers, still listening to the conductor. Vishal hopped from foot to foot, holding on. The moment the conductor stepped away, Harsha squeezed his hand. "Now. Tell me." "The bus has an ELEPHANT on it!" he said. She looked, and it did.

qa.q: What was painted on the bus?
qa.a: An elephant.

qa.q: Why did Vishal keep saying "Amma" so urgently?
qa.a: Vishal was excited and seemed afraid the elephant thought would slip away if he had to wait.

qa.q: What could other parents borrow from Harsha?
qa.a: A quiet signal like the child's hand on the arm, covered by the parent's hand, then a clear "Now, tell me" when it is the child's turn 🙂

qa.q: What was it like for Harsha when Vishal tugged her sleeve?
qa.a: Harsha needed to hear the conductor, but she stayed patient and found a way to show Vishal he would be heard soon.

grounding: Shows a small child interrupting because an exciting thought feels urgent, and a parent teaching waiting with a hand-on-arm signal instead of silencing him.
